name: Lena Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything you would keep separate from a public answer. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I wire and repair houses and businesses, about average at the trade rather than a specialist in every system. Yesterday I had to explain to a shopkeeper why a new socket wouldn't cure a damaged cable behind the wall. I like finding the actual fault, and I like a paper job sheet I can read with dirty fingers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits around the job at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a plant nursery, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn the usual trade pay, we have four months of normal expenses saved, and there are some other electrical firms nearby. I never use AI tools and don't replace a familiar method until I've got a good reason and time to understand the replacement. I prefer the actual wage, cost and result to an argument about which side of technology you're on.

say: I'd accept **quicker office invoices** while keeping the practical wiring work properly done.
I wouldn't miss being told that **familiar methods** had become embarrassing because a new tool existed.
think: I expect **work and money** to remain secure, with four months of expenses covering ordinary interruptions.
Our household can have a **decent year** without needing a dramatic change in technology.
do: Keep the usual **repair rota** and paper job sheets now and through the first plateau year.
Maintain the **household budget** rather than spend savings to appear modern.
feel: **Calm** about household living, with relief at retaining a familiar working rhythm.
S0.quote: I don't need to win a contest with a screen to finish a good job.
fieldNote: Her **calm** reflects steady work and a moderate household reserve, rather than believing that ordinary bills or quiet periods never happen.
She remains **resistant to AI** without treating a customer's question as an insult or accepting an unchecked answer as a safe instruction.

steps.text: Continue the usual repair rota and paper job sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office could make invoices quicker without giving the repair van a new personality. I'd keep doing the wiring properly. I wouldn't miss being told that every familiar method had become embarrassing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect our work and money to carry on securely in that picture. Four months of expenses gives us room for an ordinary repair bill or a short quiet patch. The household doesn't need a technology revolution to have a decent year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the usual repair rota and paper job sheets. Through the first plateau year I'd carry on the same household budget and ask for help learning a new office procedure only if the firm actually required it. I wouldn't spend savings to show I was modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and bills, with relief at keeping a rhythm I know. I'd still get annoyed by traffic and the wrong fitting in a delivery. Those are ordinary working-day problems, not fear about losing our living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a customer brought an AI answer to the repair visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the test result and explain the actual repair, rather than argue about what a program had said. A customer can ask a question without the answer becoming a safe instruction. I don't need to win a contest with a screen to finish a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more of the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave it for genuine household trouble rather than buy things because the future sounded quieter. Keeping four months available is our existing position, not a new saving action. I'd still want it if a van repair spoiled a week.

say: I'd ask the booking office to count **tests and travel** before promising a new schedule to customers.
I'd judge **actual working days** rather than a neatly filled calendar when deciding whether the plan helped.
think: My **practical paid hours** should remain steady over the next few years despite faster office planning.
Schedules designed away from repairs could still make the **working day** rushed and irritating.
do: Record **travel and repair** time on paper for one month now.
Use repeated differences to request **corrected schedules** during the first year while keeping familiar repair methods.
feel: **Uneasy** about imposed schedules, while expecting her own normal wage to continue.
S1.quote: A new form still needs a truthful record.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **working-day irritation** from expected income loss and doesn't invent a need to leave the trade immediately.
Her **response to technology** stays practical and cautious: paper evidence, corrected schedules and a request for instruction rather than independent AI use.

steps.text: Continue familiar repairs while recording actual travel and testing time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the booking office should keep the times for tests and travel in its calculations. I'd judge the new plan by the actual working day, not how neatly it filled a calendar. I wouldn't want to spend the evening correcting an impossible promise to a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My practical work should keep my normal paid hours steady for the next few years. But I would be uneasy about schedules set by people who hadn't watched a repair. A wage can be secure while the day becomes more irritating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd record the actual travel and repair time for a month on paper. In the first year I'd bring any repeated difference from the booking plan to the manager and ask for a corrected schedule. I'd keep the familiar repair methods rather than start using AI to avoid seeming old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pace being imposed, not afraid of losing the wage in this picture. I'd want a sensible answer about the time a job takes. I wouldn't need a new career plan because the office bought software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the manager about an impossible schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd point to the missed travel or testing time in the last month's jobs. If it wasn't in the plan, it would still happen in the real day. I'd rather have that discussion before the customer was waiting in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an unfamiliar electronic record became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what paid teaching and checking came with it before using it. I wouldn't quietly invent a result to keep the office happy. A new form still needs a truthful record.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 and continue repairs while they remained paid.
I wouldn't claim the **three-year gap** protects the whole rest of my working life.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink as firms prepare to use capable hands-on robots.
Four months of **bills saved** cannot replace the mortgage contribution, especially when unfamiliar work takes me time to learn.
do: Add a small **savings transfer** only while paid hours hold and money remains after essentials.
Check hours monthly after 2028, applying if they fall and leaving only after a signed **better repair offer** after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with savings and reachable employers providing a cautious plan.
S2.quote: The point is a useful reserve, not a savings figure made out of debt.
fieldNote: She rejects **debt-funded saving** and keeps the transfer conditional on maintained hours and an actual surplus after household essentials.
Her **job-search trigger** is falling paid hours, while course questions remain enquiries rather than an invented retraining commitment.

steps.text: Save a small wage amount only while hours hold and essentials leave surplus
Check paid repair hours monthly before deciding whether to seek another job
Seek better signed repair offer after travel if hours fall, before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking work changes in 2028, with capable hands-on robots following around 2031. I'd still do the repairs while they were paid. I wouldn't turn a three-year gap into a claim that my whole career was protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink as firms prepared to use robots for more of the work. Four months of bills would be a buffer, not a replacement for the wage that pays our mortgage. I'd worry about having to learn another way of earning when change comes slowly to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd postpone the planned living-room furniture replacement and redirect a small part of each wage into the reserve while paid hours held. In the first year after 2028 I'd check my actual paid repair hours monthly before deciding whether to seek another job. If the hours fell, I'd apply for posted repair roles with better written pay after travel and leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible income loss, but with a plan that didn't require pretending I'd become enthusiastic overnight. I'd have a reserve and some nearby employers to check. I'd still wish I could keep improving the same familiar work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the extra saving affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set the extra transfer at a small amount left after essentials, not force it by borrowing elsewhere. If paid hours or the surplus fell, I'd reduce the transfer. The point is a useful reserve, not a savings figure made out of debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for retraining straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what the work was and what paid practical teaching came with it. I haven't chosen or funded another course. I wouldn't use the mortgage buffer for an advert promising a permanently safe job.

say: I'd use **five years** to keep bills paid while watching the actual work, rather than guess at every change.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** visible and continue checking what they meant for the real repair day.
think: I expect **steady practical years** before direct hands-on competition becomes pressing on my paid hours.
That gives time to strengthen the **reserve**, while unfamiliar later systems would still make me uneasy.
do: Postpone the **furniture purchase** and add savings only while paid hours hold and essentials leave a surplus.
Check **paid hours** monthly after 2031 before deciding whether a job move is needed.
Seek a signed **better repair offer** after travel if hours fall, remaining in the current job until then.
feel: **Uneasy** about later career changes, while secure about near-term household bills and practical work.
S3.quote: Being prepared can include staying where the actual wage still works.
fieldNote: The **slower timeline** changes her expectation of near-term paid work, without weakening the eventual capable-robot endpoint.
Her **cautious plan** leaves course decisions open and treats continued useful paid work as evidence rather than a failure to react.

steps.text: Save a small wage amount only while hours hold and essentials leave surplus
Check paid repair hours monthly before deciding whether to seek another job
Seek better signed repair offer after travel if hours fall, before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to keep the bills paid and watch what actually happens to the trade. I'd still put the robots around 2034 on the calendar. More time doesn't mean I can stop checking the real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I expect more steady practical years before hands-on competition becomes pressing. That gives us time to strengthen the reserve without pretending we can live on it forever. I'd still be uneasy about learning a different system later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd postpone the furniture and add the same small savings transfer only while paid hours held and essentials left a surplus. In the first year after 2031 I'd check paid hours monthly before any job change. If hours fell, I'd apply for posted repair work with better written pay after travel, staying until a signed offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual career, but secure about household living over the next few years. I'd value time to repeat a new task if I actually needed it. I wouldn't suddenly want to learn through AI because the date had moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your pay and repair hours held throughout the preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep the transfer affordable and keep doing the repairs. I wouldn't force a change of job to prove I had used the warning. Being prepared can include staying where the actual wage still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm later required a new practical skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what task was being required and who would show it during paid work. A discussion about teaching isn't enrollment in another career. I'd want the costs and practical supervision before choosing anything.

say: I'd use **ten years** to make careful decisions from facts, checking those facts each year.
I wouldn't empty the **savings account** on guesses simply because the warning period was long.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume retirement income would replace wages when hands-on robots followed.
Present pay, our **reserve and alternatives** make near-term household bills look secure while later choices remain open.
do: Maintain the **furniture delay** and save only while paid hours hold and essentials leave a surplus.
Check **paid hours** monthly after 2036 before deciding whether to seek different work.
Seek a signed **better repair offer** after travel if hours fall, changing only after the offer exists.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual change, while settled about near-term household living and able to inspect actual offers.
S4.quote: My caution isn't a plan for my children to pay our mortgage.
fieldNote: She makes **no future-income assumption** from retirement age or older children, keeping the household wage need distinct from hoped-for resources.
Her **waiting has triggers** through checked paid hours and actual vacancies, with an earlier search if income begins falling before the date.

steps.text: Keep the living-room furniture replacement postponed
Save a small wage amount only while hours hold and essentials leave surplus
Check paid repair hours monthly before deciding whether to seek another job
Seek better signed repair offer after travel if hours fall, before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to make careful decisions when the facts turn up. I'd still want the facts checked each year. A long warning isn't a reason to empty a savings account on guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 56 when hands-on robots followed. I couldn't assume we'd stop needing wages then, even if the children were grown. Our present pay, four-month reserve and some other employers make the next few years look secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the furniture postponed and the small transfer going only while hours held and essentials left a surplus. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare actual paid repair hours monthly before choosing a move. If they fell, I'd seek a signed repair offer with better written pay after travel before leaving this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual change, but settled about the household for the next few years. I'd have time to look at a real offer instead of buying a general promise. I wouldn't confuse being 56 with having a retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the decade change plans for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't choose their studies from a card or count their wages in our future budget. I'd ask them to look at actual work and what it took to learn. My caution isn't a plan for my children to pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep careful waiting from turning into ignoring change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd review actual paid hours, the reserve and reachable vacancies each year. If pay started falling, I'd look earlier rather than wait for 2036. I'd keep the change tied to facts I could check.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose hours before I'd understood what useful work came next. Clear written paid hours and practical teaching from a person, if a new skill was needed, would help. I'd rather check one real offer than pay for ten comforting predictions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether waiting has a date and a reason. I'm slow to change, but I can still watch my paid hours and act if they fall. I don't want being careful mistaken for not noticing.

headlineQuote: I'd rather check one real offer than pay for ten comforting predictions.
portrait: **Lena, 43**, is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, typical trade pay and ordinary practical skills.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage, four months of expenses saved and some nearby electrical employers.
She **never uses AI**, prefers paper job sheets and judges changes through actual paid hours, costs and checked results.
Fast competition creates **income anxiety**; slower preparation supports affordable saving and monitored waiting without assumed retirement or children's earnings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her paid hours before she understands the next useful earning route.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **written paid hours** would support household planning.
Practical **in-person teaching** would help if new skills became necessary.
